item.title: Refugee Convention at 75: Protecting Journalists-in-Exile
item.description:
On 28 July 1951, the UK was one of 11 founding signatories to the UN Refugee Convention – the charter which has protected millions forced to flee persecution. 75 years on, that protection has never been more important for journalists.

For freelancers, exile is no longer an exceptional consequence of reporting the truth. It is increasingly becoming part of the job. Since the Taliban seized power in Afghanistan in 2021, the number of countries from which freelance journalists have sought support has doubled.  Today, forced displacement is the single biggest reason journalists seek assistance from the Rory Peck Trust. Freelancers from Gaza, Myanmar, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Afghanistan now make up a growing proportion of those we support.

Unlike staff journalists, they don’t have an employer to arrange an evacuation, provide legal advice or continue paying a salary while they rebuild their lives. When they flee, they often do so alone. They must navigate asylum systems, secure visas and prove their professional status without the backing of a recognised news organisation. At precisely the moment they are most vulnerable, they are also the most unsupported.

Anosha knows this all too well. She fled Afghanistan after receiving repeated threats from the Taliban because of her reporting on women’s rights and human rights. Age 25, now living in Pakistan, she received support from the Rory Peck Trust to cover essential living costs and move to safer accommodation, enabling her to continue reporting from exile.

However, crossing a border rarely ends the danger. Authoritarian governments increasingly extend their reach beyond their own frontiers, intimidating, surveilling and threatening journalists who continue reporting from abroad. Repressive laws, including so-called ‘foreign agent’ legislation, are being used to criminalise independent journalism, even in exile. Alongside these threats come the daily realities of displacement: uncertain immigration status, financial hardship, language barriers and separation from the sources, colleagues and communities that made reporting possible.

Albert is an investigative journalist specialising in organised crime and human rights abuses in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He was forced to flee after M23 rebels targeted him and threatened his family. The Rory Peck Trust helped him relocate to neighbouring Burundi and replace equipment destroyed during the attack. “I feel relieved,” he says. “I feel better now and am able to continue my work remotely.”

His experience is increasingly common. Many journalists continue reporting on their home countries from exile because the story does not become less important simply because the reporter has crossed a border. If anything, the need for trusted reporting often becomes even greater.

It is why, from September, we are launching the Rory Peck Scholarship. In partnership with City St George’s, University of London, the scholarship will fund one journalist in exile to study for a Master’s degree in International Journalism, helping them rebuild a professional future, expand their networks and continue their reporting far from home.

“Independent journalism is one of our strongest defences against disinformation and propaganda.” says Jon Williams, Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust. “Supporting journalists-in-exile is not simply a humanitarian responsibility, it is an investment in the future of truth itself. Because when independent journalists are forced into silence, we all lose access to the facts that help us understand the world.”

75 years ago, the Refugee Convention gave the world a framework for protecting those forced to flee. Today, our challenge is to ensure that protection does not mark the end of a journalist’s career, but the beginning of the next chapter. Ensuring freelancers can continue reporting in exile means the truth does not become another casualty.

Something worth protecting—for the next 75 years and beyond

The names of individuals have been changed to protect their safety

item.title: New scholarship for journalists-in-exile
item.description:
The Rory Peck Trust has launched a new scholarship to help freelance journalists-in-exile rebuild their careers in the UK.

Thousands of journalists around the world have been driven from their home countries because of their reporting. Some have been expelled by governments; others have fled persecution, arbitrary detention or threats to their lives. The number forced into exile has risen sharply in recent years. Around half of the journalists seeking support from the Rory Peck Trust today are freelancers who have either fled their countries or are trying to escape. While many hope their exile will be temporary, the reality is often very different: what begins as a short-term refuge can become a permanent reality.

In a series of workshops hosted by the Trust, exiled journalists now living in the UK told how all faced significant barriers to continuing their careers. Qualifications were not always recognised, professional networks had disappeared, and many struggled to gain a foothold in the UK media industry. So, from September, the Rory Peck Trust is partnering with City St George’s, University of London, to enable one journalist-in-exile to complete an M.A. in International Journalism.

Jon Williams, Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, said: “For many of those, their journalism is the reason they are here. They have been forced to flee after exposing stories others wanted kept hidden. They are talented, courageous journalists who simply need the opportunity to demonstrate what they can do. This scholarship will help them rebuild their careers, create new professional networks and ensure their journalism has a future, thousands of miles from home.”

The intensive one-year Master’s programme combines practical training across broadcast, print and digital journalism with advanced study of international reporting, equipping students with the skills needed for today’s global media landscape. Dr Zahera Harb, Director of Postgraduate Studies at City St George’s, knows first-hand the challenges faced by journalists forced to leave home. Before moving to the UK, she spent more than a decade reporting and presenting in Lebanon. She said: “We’re incredibly excited about this partnership with the Rory Peck Trust and the opportunities it will create to support journalists in exile. It will equip them with the knowledge, professional networks and global perspective needed to build a successful career, helping them overcome the professional disruption caused by displacement and exile.”

Applicants must be freelance journalists living in exile, displaced, or at risk because of their journalism. They must meet City St George’s academic and English language entry requirements and hold an immigration status that permits study in the UK. Applications are now open via the button below, with the inaugural Rory Peck Scholar to be announced in September.

Williams hopes the scholarship will become the first step in a broader programme of support for journalists forced into exile. “Journalism is built on community as much as competition. Journalists rely on one another for advice, support and shared experience. That sense of professional solidarity becomes even more important when someone has been forced to leave everything behind. This scholarship is about more than education. It’s about helping outstanding journalists belong again – about protecting independent journalism.”

If you will help fund the study of a journalist-in-exile, please click here.

item.title: Rory Peck “A Lifeline” in Journalism’s Deadliest Year
item.description:
More than 430 freelance journalists received support from the Rory Peck Trust last year, as record levels of conflict and violence placed unprecedented pressure on independent journalism around the world.

The Trust’s newly published Impact Report details the growing demands faced by freelance journalists in 2025 — the deadliest year on record for the profession, with 129 journalists and media workers killed globally, many of them freelancers.

More than 250 people received safety and first aid training through the Trust during the year, while applications to the Rory Peck Trust Crisis Fund continued to rise sharply. The number of freelancers supported through emergency assistance grants increased by more than 12%.

Dozens more received trauma therapy and psychological support after covering conflict and crisis — assistance the Trust says is critical not only to recovery, but to ensuring experienced journalists are able to continue working.

Many of those supported were based in the Middle East and North Africa. Nearly half of all crisis grants awarded in 2025 went to Palestinian journalists in Gaza, while 44 freelance journalists in Lebanon received hostile environment and first aid training.

The report also highlights the Trust’s growing advocacy work on journalist safety and impunity, including engagement with policymakers in the UK and overseas, and convening discussions on the protection of journalists at a time of rapidly deteriorating press freedom worldwide.

Alongside operational data, the report includes personal testimonies from freelancers supported by the Trust during the year.

Jon Williams, Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, said:

“In journalism’s darkest hour, thanks to the generosity of our supporters, the Rory Peck Trust has been a lifeline for freelancers from Palestine to Mexico, Britain, Bangladesh and beyond.

“It can mean the difference between a journalist getting out alive, a freelancer in exile being able to continue working, or trauma being treated rather than ignored — at a time when that support is needed more than ever.”

You can read the 2026 Impact Report here.

item.title: Press Freedom’s Traffic Lights “Flashing Red”
item.description:
Governments must act to end the killing of journalists and tackle what he described as “staggering” levels of impunity, the Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust has said.

Speaking to the BBC on World Press Freedom Day, Jon Williams warned that those responsible for attacks on journalists—particularly in Gaza—must be held to account, including individuals indicted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes.

Last year was the deadliest on record for journalism, with 129 journalists and media workers killed worldwide. More than 260 Palestinian journalists have been killed in Gaza over the past two and a half years.

Click to watch BBC News interview

International law recognises journalists as civilians, making their deliberate targeting a war crime. But Williams warned that those protections are being ignored.

“We wouldn’t tolerate this if people ignored the traffic lights… something would happen.” he said. “That is exactly what is going on around the world. The lights are flashing red, and governments are ignoring the traffic lights which are flashing red and saying democracy is in danger, because journalism is in danger.”

Williams’ comments followed the publication of the latest Global Press Freedom Index, published by Reporters Without Borders, which recorded the lowest level of media freedom in its 25-year history. In more than half of all countries, press freedom is now classified as “difficult” or “very serious”. A quarter of a century ago, around 20% of the world’s population lived in countries rated “good” for press freedom; today, that figure has fallen to less than 1%.

Click to watch ‘Isa Soares Tonight’, CNN

Earlier, in an interview with CNN’s Isa Soares, Jon Williams said the world was now a fight to defend the truth, warning “if we have no truth, we have no freedom”. He was speaking as he and Soares toured the Trust’s photo exhibition, ‘Being There’ in London.

On Sunday, more than 50 visitors joined a special World Press Freedom Day discussion in the exhibition space on the threats facing independent journalism around the world. Palestinian journalist Yousef Hammash, British-Iranian reporter Sahar Zand, and Kurdish journalist Hilal Sevenn – all Rory Peck Trust alumni – told how the risks facing freelancers had increased in scale, range and complexity while the response had not.

From left, Hilal Sevenn, Sahar Zand & Yousef Hammash talk with Jon Williams

‘Being There: Witness, Truth and Trust’, produced in partnership with international news agencies AFP, AP and Reuters, drew around 500 visitors over its run at London’s ST.ART Gallery. As it closed on Sunday evening, Williams said the level of public engagement had been striking.

“At a time when journalism is under real pressure, that response matters.” he said, describing the support shown by visitors as “extraordinary”.

item.title: Journalism’s Deadliest Year In Pictures
item.description:
Five days before World Press Freedom Day, a photo exhibition has opened in London telling the story of journalism’s deadliest year, through the images that defined it.

Being There” Witness Trust and Trust has been curated by the Rory Peck Trust in partnership with AFP, AP and Reuters as well as London’s ST.ART Galley. Among the pictures featured is an image captured by a Palestinian journalist just two days before she was killed by an Israeli airstrike.

Freelance photojournalism Mariam Dagga from Gaza, worked with the Associated Press. On Saturday in August 2025, she captured a scene that became all too familiar: a family mourning their 11-year-old son inside the hospital. Two days later, in that same place, Mariam was killed in an airstrike. She was just 33 years old.

At least 129 journalists and media workers were killed last year – and the exhibition tells not just the story of the past year, but the stories behind the stories. Many of those featured are freelancers. They take the risks. They make the judgement calls. And too often, they do it without the backing or protection staff journalists rely on.

But this exhibition isn’t just about them.

In a moment where journalism is under sustained pressure and misinformation moves faster than fact, the exhibitions shows that the  images are not just pictures. They are the product of presence, judgement, and often, courage. Speaking at the opening of the exhibition last night, the Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, Jon Williams said he hoped it would change the way people think about frontline journalism. “When you see just what it takes to be there—you don’t just see these images differently. You value them differently. And that matters. Because if we don’t value eyewitness journalism, we won’t defend it. And if we don’t defend it, we risk losing it.”

Being There: Witness Truth and Trust runs until Sunday. You can also visit the exhibition by clicking on the button below.

Open daily 12-6pm, ST.ART Gallery, 36 Eastcastle St, London. W1W 8DP. Admission free.

The post Journalism’s Deadliest Year In Pictures appeared first on Rory Peck Trust.

item.title: UK Memorial to Honour Journalists Killed on Frontlines
item.description:
An acclaimed British artist is to design the UK’s first permanent memorial to those killed while gathering the news. Wolfgang Buttress will create a permanent artwork at the National Memorial Arboretum in Staffordshire, with a companion piece at London’s St Bride’s Church in Fleet Street.

More than 100 artists entered a design competition run by the Royal Society of Sculptors to commemorate British and UK‑based journalists and media workers killed while bearing witness to conflict.  Buttress’s winning design, End of Copy | Words of Light, was unveiled by the Foreign Office Minister Chris Elmore MP at an event at Bloomberg Space in Central London this evening attended by news industry leaders and the families of journalists killed while reporting.

Buttress’s winning design was praised by the judges for its emotional intelligence, restraint and enduring relevance, and for inviting contemplation without spectacle. The panel included the Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, Jon Wiliams, who is a Trustee of the charity building the memorial.

Speaking after the announcement, Wolfgang Buttress said: “Journalism at its best is an act of service, often quiet, frequently risky and, in the most tragic cases, fatal. My ambition was to create a work that acknowledges loss while leaving space for reflection, humility and care.”

Last year was the deadliest ever for journalists. 129 members of the media were killed according to figures compiled by the Committee to Protect Journalists.

Since 2000, 16 UK journalists have been killed reporting the news. Introducing Buttress’s winning design, Jon Williams said they deserved to be remembered properly, publicly and permanently: “This memorial will say, what, too often, we fail to say ourselves: That journalism matters, that truth matters. And that those who risk everything to ensure our right to know and protect our freedom—must not—and will not be forgotten.”

The memorial is expected to be installed at the National Memorial Arboretum once fundraising and permissions are complete, while the proposed online record will be created and then continue to grow as families contribute stories, images and testimony.

The post UK Memorial to Honour Journalists Killed on Frontlines appeared first on Rory Peck Trust.

item.title: Exhibition to Show Reality of Reporting After Deadliest Year
item.description:
Images from the world’s frontlines will go on public display in London later this month in an exhibition that shows the escalating risks faced by freelancers— and the growing cost of bearing witness.

‘Being There: Witness, Truth & Trust’, is being staged to mark World Press Freedom Day on 3rd May. It tells the story of the past 12 months through its defining photographs— many taken in conflict zones where journalists are increasingly targeted, discredited and killed.

Last year was the deadliest year on record for journalism. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, at least 129 journalists and media workers were killed around the world.

 

Mariam Dagga, was a freelance photojournalist, based in Gaza. She was among 20 people, including five journalists, killed in an Israeli airstrike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital last August.  Three days before she was killed, she captured one family’s grief at 13-year-old Karim Qdei’s funeral in Khan Younis, an image featured in the exhibition.

 

Hussam al-Masri, a Reuters cameraman was also killed in the attack along with Al Jazeera journalists, Mohammed Salama, freelancer Moaz Abu Taha, and Ahmed Abu Aziz. The United Nations says more than 200 Palestinian journalists have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war with Israel.

 

 

The exhibition also features the image of the former Prince Andrew leaving a Thames Valley Police station earlier this year. Taken by Reuters photographer Phil Noble, the picture made front pages worldwide and has become one of the defining news images of the year. It will be shown publicly for the first time.

At a time when disinformation is on the rise and trust in journalism falling, the exhibition makes a direct case for eyewitness reporting — showing not just the images that shape global understanding, but the reality of how they are obtained: the courage, commitment and sacrifice.

Jon Williams, Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, said: “Journalists are being killed in record numbers.

 “There has never been a more dangerous time to be a journalist. Every day we see the courage and resilience of those reporting from the world’s frontlines. This exhibition is about showing what it really takes to bear witness and why that work matters – about truth and trust. Both depend on journalists willing to take risks on our behalf. Lose that, and we lose our ability to understand the world as it really is.”

Produced in partnership with AFP, The Associated Press,  Reuters and ST.ART Gallery, the exhibition will run from Wednesday 29 April until Sunday 3rd May. It is open daily from 12pm to 6pm. Admission is free.

item.content:encoded:
Images from the world’s frontlines will go on public display in London later this month in an exhibition that shows the escalating risks faced by freelancers— and the growing cost of bearing witness.

‘Being There: Witness, Truth & Trust’, is being staged to mark World Press Freedom Day on 3rd May. It tells the story of the past 12 months through its defining photographs— many taken in conflict zones where journalists are increasingly targeted, discredited and killed.

Last year was the deadliest year on record for journalism. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, at least 129 journalists and media workers were killed around the world.

 

Mariam Dagga, was a freelance photojournalist, based in Gaza. She was among 20 people, including five journalists, killed in an Israeli airstrike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital last August.  Three days before she was killed, she captured one family’s grief at 13-year-old Karim Qdei’s funeral in Khan Younis, an image featured in the exhibition.

 

Hussam al-Masri, a Reuters cameraman was also killed in the attack along with Al Jazeera journalists, Mohammed Salama, freelancer Moaz Abu Taha, and Ahmed Abu Aziz. The United Nations says more than 200 Palestinian journalists have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war with Israel.

 

 

The exhibition also features the image of the former Prince Andrew leaving a Thames Valley Police station earlier this year. Taken by Reuters photographer Phil Noble, the picture made front pages worldwide and has become one of the defining news images of the year. It will be shown publicly for the first time.

At a time when disinformation is on the rise and trust in journalism falling, the exhibition makes a direct case for eyewitness reporting — showing not just the images that shape global understanding, but the reality of how they are obtained: the courage, commitment and sacrifice.

Jon Williams, Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, said: “Journalists are being killed in record numbers.

 “There has never been a more dangerous time to be a journalist. Every day we see the courage and resilience of those reporting from the world’s frontlines. This exhibition is about showing what it really takes to bear witness and why that work matters – about truth and trust. Both depend on journalists willing to take risks on our behalf. Lose that, and we lose our ability to understand the world as it really is.”

Produced in partnership with AFP, The Associated Press,  Reuters and ST.ART Gallery, the exhibition will run from Wednesday 29 April until Sunday 3rd May. It is open daily from 12pm to 6pm. Admission is free.

item.title: Three Journalists Targeted And Killed In Israeli Airstrilke
item.description:
The Rory Peck Trust has condemned the killing of three journalists in an Israeli airstrike in southern Lebanon,

Ali Shoaib, a correspondent for the Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Manar TV, was killed on Saturday alongside reporter Fatima Ftouni and her brother, Mohamad, a freelance photojournalist. The siblings worked for the Lebanese news channel, Al-Mayadeen. In a statement, the channel said the three journalists had been travelling in a vehicle clearly marked “Press” when it was hit by four missiles.

The Israel said it had targeted Shoaib because he was a Hezbollah intelligence operative. However, the Israeli Defence Force did not immediately provide any evidence to support the allegation. Israel has not commented on the deaths of the other two journalists.

The Rory Peck Trust says it is deeply concerned by the escalation of Israel’s war in Lebanon. Its Executive Director, Jonn Williams, fears there is a troubling pattern to the attacks:

“It is the same old story: journalists smeared, allegations of terrorism but no hard evidence. Journalists are civilians. They are protected under international law, and targeting them is a war crime. Since 7 October 2023, Israel has killed more than 200 members of the media in Gaza. It cannot be allowed to do so in Lebanon.”

Lebanese officials have condemned the airstrike as a “blatant crime”. The country’s President, Joseph Aoun, said the attack violated international protections afforded to journalists in conflict. Two days ago another journalist, freelance photographer Hussain Hamood, was killed in an Israeli air strike while he was filming in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh. He too was working for Al-Manar at the time of his death.

item.title: Tributes To Paul Conroy, The Photographer Who Refused To Look Away
item.description:
Tributes have been paid to the photographer and freelance journalist Paul Conroy, who has died from a heart attack. He was 61 and had just returned from Cuba, where he had been reporting on the aftermath of the arrest of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by the United States.

In 2012 Paul was critically injured in the attack that killed his Sunday Times colleague Marie Colvin and French photojournalist Rémi Ochlik during the siege of Homs. Smuggled out of Syria alongside fellow journalist Édith Bouvier, he endured five months in hospital in the UK, undergoing 23 operations on his leg as well as surgery to his abdomen and back.

Paul documented his ordeal in ‘Under the Wire’, a searing account of survival, journalism and the moral imperative to bear witness. In 2018, the book was made into a movie, starring Jamie Dornan as Paul. ‘A Private War’ introduced a wider audience to the realities freelance journalists face in war zones.

Alan Conroy has led the tributes to his brother, telling how Paul found deep satisfaction in exposing injustice: “I think he’ll be proud to say, ‘I’ve done my bit, my conscience is clear. I actually did something about it’.” RPT Trustee and BBC presenter, Clive Myrie, described him as “a wonderful photojournalist and a wonderful human being… a decent, principled and kind man” while Channel 4 News International Editor, Lindsey Hilsum, said: “All of us who knew and loved him are devastated.”

Paul had covered conflicts in Libya, Afghanistan and the Democratic Republic of Congo as well as Syria. Most recently he had been based in Ukraine. Two decades after receiving a hostile environment training bursary from the Rory Peck Trust, Paul was training Ukrainian journalists in battlefield first aid — passing on the skills that had once helped save his own life — while continuing to document the war’s toll on civilians.

The Executive Director of the Rory Peck Trust, Jon Williams,  said “Even at the end of his life Paul was doing what he had always done: travelling towards the story not away from it. For those of us who believe journalism matters, his life stands as a reminder of what that belief looks like in practice. He showed up. He stayed. He bore witness.”

Paul Conroy is survived by his wife, three sons and grandchildren.

item.title: International media steps up its campaign to access Gaza
item.description:
Foreign journalists based in Israel and the Palestinian Territories have stepped up their campaign calling on Israel to lift its ban on independent reporting from Gaza. The Foreign Press Association has launched an online petition and an online video, urging audiences around the world to stand up for their right to be informed.

The video, featuring some of the biggest names in international news, urges Isarael to “let us in”,  describing its ban as “unprecedented”. The journalists say their Palestinian colleagues have been working under impossible conditions, and shouldn’t have to bear the burden alone. “For more than two years, Israel has the barred foreign press from entering Gaza to report freely” says the FPA: “this ban is an affront to press freedoms and the public’s right to information.”

CLICK TO WATCH THE VIDEO IN FULL

The campaign, supported by the Rory Peck Trust, comes as Israel’s Supreme Court declined to order Israel’s government to reverse the ban. The FPA says “at every turn, Israel has responded with stalling tactics and vague security arguments along with a refusal to engage in dialogue”. Israel and Egypt have prevented independent press access to Gaza since the beginning of the war. It has, however, facilitated reporting from inside Gaza by those embedded with the IDF.

Israel claims the presence of journalists would pose security risks to IDF soldiers and to the journalists themselves. News organisations say they are best placed to manage the risks faced by their teams.
